children.author: bpeng2000
children.text:
Personal experience:

AI tends to add new wheels for a new feature in a large codebase, because finding, understanding, and generalizing the existing code to integrate a new feature will likely break existing features, cost more effort (and token) to implement and test. Human reviewers also tend to like these code since they are clean, easy to review, and get the job done, especially when they are not familiar with existing codebase.

The issue is that wheels like these accumulate in the codebase, and they inevitably entangle. When an upstream specification changes, when a new feature that works with many existing features are introduced, all these wheels need to be revisited, and in many cases they are not because the new test cases do not cover all the paths. The code base got larger and more complex, and contains more bugs than the unit tests can cover, especially when unit tests are often "bent" to fit the wrong behavior unnoticed.

I see the same in e.g. simple CSS. I ask ChatGPT to apply styling X to aĺl instances of say a UI control type. Then to another. Later I ask for a tweak of X. Bot updates some but not all instances. It didn't create a single class for all. No intelligence seen.

The most remarkable fails are simpler though. E.g. at version 303 I ask "Revert to version 299". I get 299 with 303's edits. Bot explains it interpreted "Revert" to mean something no intelligent programmer would.

And most importantly, these are just the ones I directly notice. To see the total, I have to read through and understand the most repulsive code I've seen in my life.

The only way to be satisfied with bot code is by having exceptionally low expectations. And never ever let yourself be kidded that your helper is more than a stochastic parrot gorged on stackoverflow etc.

I've been working on a large (~10MLOC) mostly vibe-coded project for months now. It's actually quite frustrating:

* The agent will fix a bug when I tell it to, but only in exactly one place. I'll notice that another place has that bug later and have to redo it. It's the sort of thing that I would know to check for if I were fixing it myself. Yes, I can ask it to look elsewhere for similar bugs, but even that's not super reliable.

* The user-facing text it generates is just as awkward as ever. I have to rewrite all of it, and sometimes it slips through. It's also hard to write text when you don't know what the code is actually doing.

* It doesn't have a good model of what kind of information is relevant to humans. It's just as likely to produce a paragraph of random jargon as a clear explanation of what's actually going on. It shows excessive detail for things that don't matter, and not enough detail for things that do. For example, it doesn't understand that $0 can logically mean "null" in terms of how humans think about things (e.g. "This item is free" vs. "This item is $0").

I kind of wish I hadn't gone down this path but now it's far too late, I can't really manually maintain this amount of slop. I'm quite sad if this is going to be the end state of this profession.

My advice is to start a totally vibe coded side project. You will never gain confidence until you experiment, find the failure cases, learn to deal with them, etc.

Choose something you want to do but don't really care that much about. Be more ambitious than you think you could be, have a high bar on the outcome but purposefully choose to completely ignore the actual code. I really like those videos too, but a very big difference is, in manufacturing QA, the system outputs a very high number of copies of a very small number of possible types, so spot checks work fine from an operations research point of view, as the variance in output has a known upper bound.

For code, I think things go in the opposite direction: the system outputs artifacts that are all different among themselves (even more so now that we no longer distribute software via physical copies. Well, bits are always physical, but I mean we no longer ship floppies/CDs/DVDs).

The furious pace of Ux “optimisation” that we see across the board (and especially at AI companies) is a hidden anti pattern. The time and frustration of learning a new ux is an acceptable burden when it frames real new capabilities or workflows. It’s not good to rework your ux user experience every week just because you can.

Not only that, but AI is categorically terrible at ux review. I don’t mean aesthetics, I mean attention flow, workflow in general and what the user anticipates as a logical path to feature discovery and exploration. Increasingly, features are hidden behind workflows that meet a single use case but fail to be universally logical or in many cases, even accessible at all outside of the test case.

So, people… use AI in code review. It’s actually pretty great at it if you do it right, and you can ship better software with fewer bugs than ever before. But please, don’t pressure your ux guy to “10x” with AI.
